credit: SAC Faye Storer / UK Ministry of Defence · Crown copyright / Open Government Licence v1.0 · resized
alt: Snow patches and dark exposed ground across the Cairngorm mountains, with an RAF rescue helicopter in the foreground.
caption: Winter in the Cairngorms during a rescue-training flight. Bright snow reflects more sunlight than the darker exposed ground; patchy cover changes the landscape's albedo.

credit: Steve Redman / US National Park Service · public domain · resized
alt: Snow-covered Mount Adams viewed from the Naches Loop Trail in Washington.
caption: Mount Adams, Washington. This Cascade arc volcano is part of the volcanic chain above the Cascadia subduction zone.

credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

credit: Rich Keen / DPRA / USFWS · public domain · resized
alt: Denver's skyline and distant mountain slopes seen from Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge.
caption: Denver, Colorado. The city stands on high plains beside the Rocky Mountains; elevation reduces air pressure compared with sea level.

credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
caption: Texas Panhandle during the Dust Bowl. Wind removed exposed topsoil during severe drought; this photograph records dust in the air, rather than water-cut gullies.

credit: Giuseppe Milo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
alt: Waves and wet sand beneath Naples Pier on Florida's Gulf coast at sunset.
caption: Naples, Florida. Waves redistribute sediment along a low sandy coast.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 metres east of this line.

credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
caption: Kīlauea, 25 February 1983. USGS photographed a lava fountain approximately 10 metres high; molten rock is at the surface, not throughout the mantle.

credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore transport supplies a spit at the Humber estuary.

credit: Cypp0847 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Slope failures above the coast at Hong Kong's Redhill Peninsula after extreme rainfall.
caption: Redhill Peninsula, Hong Kong. Slope failures following extreme rainfall show how saturated ground can destabilise steep developed slopes.

credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

credit: Lewis Clarke / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: White chalk cliffs, offshore remnants and a wave-cut base near the Pinnacles in Purbeck.
caption: The Pinnacles coast, Purbeck, Dorset. Erosion leaves isolated stacks and lower remnants called stumps beside the retreating chalk cliffs.

credit: NOAA Corps aerial survey: Mark Moran, Phil Eastman and Dave Demers · public domain · 2005 · resized
alt: Flooded streets and houses in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
caption: New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, 2005. Floodwater filled low-lying neighbourhoods after storm surge and flood-protection failures.

credit: Шелковников Евгений Анатольевич / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Aerial view of abandoned buildings at the Kola Superdeep Borehole site in Russia in 2020.
caption: Kola Superdeep Borehole site, 2020. The deepest borehole reached 12.262 km within continental crust; it did not enter the mantle.

credit: Stephen Poole from Malton, England / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A winding road descends Honister Pass through steep slopes in Cumbria.
caption: Honister Pass, Cumbria. Glacial erosion has shaped the mountain valleys and passes.

credit: Till Niermann (User:Till.niermann) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Dry, deeply dissected loess slopes near Hunyuan in Shanxi, China.
caption: Loess near Hunyuan, Shanxi. Wind deposited the silt; runoff later cut gullies into the exposed ground.

credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Visitors and a park ranger stand in the broad limestone Broadway passage of Mammoth Cave, Kentucky.
caption: Broadway passage, Mammoth Cave, Kentucky. Groundwater dissolution enlarged fractures in limestone into a large cave system.

credit: David Brossard / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: The Mississippi River and Natchez–Vidalia Bridge seen from Natchez, Mississippi.
caption: Natchez, Mississippi. A broad river corridor runs below the bluffs along the state's western boundary.

credit: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Aerial view of Bodie Island, its lighthouse, wetlands and Atlantic beach in North Carolina.
caption: Bodie Island, North Carolina. A low barrier island separates Atlantic waves from sheltered wetlands.

credit: Robert693 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Phoenix's skyline, transport surfaces and desert mountains seen from Sky Harbor airport.
caption: Phoenix, Arizona. Built surfaces store heat in a desert city. Air or thermal measurements are needed to quantify the urban heat island; this photograph shows the land cover.

credit: Carol M. Highsmith · The Jon B. Lovelace Collection of California Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division · public domain · resized
alt: Aerial view of the San Andreas Fault cutting across dry hills in California.
caption: San Andreas Fault in California's Sierra Madre Mountains. The fault accommodates mainly horizontal motion between the Pacific and North American plates.

credit: David290 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: The Huangpu River curves around Lujiazui's towers in Shanghai.
caption: Shanghai. Dense urban development occupies low delta ground beside the tidal Huangpu River.

credit: Petersrockypics / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Snow on Gallt y Wenallt above mist in Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia.
caption: Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia. A glacial valley lies beneath the steep Snowdon horseshoe.

credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
caption: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium. The phase is nearly the same for observers in Wales and California at the same instant; local rise times and the disc's orientation differ.

credit: Rodw / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Floodwater surrounds Burrowbridge in the Somerset Levels in February 2014.
caption: Burrowbridge, Somerset, February 2014. Low relief slows the drainage of extensive floodwater.

credit: Eirian Evans / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: The Thames Barrier's silver piers beside the tidal river in London.
caption: Thames Barrier, London. Movable gates reduce tidal-surge flood risk upstream; they do not remove every source of river or surface-water flooding.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
caption: GOES-East observes the Americas from a fixed orbital longitude. Earth's rotation underlies the daily cycle; civil time-zone boundaries are agreed conventions and are not visible in this satellite image.

credit: EOSDIS Worldview / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Satellite view of Typhoon Mangkhut with a compact eye and spiralling cloud bands in September 2018.
caption: Typhoon Mangkhut, September 2018, observed by NASA EOSDIS. The western North Pacific storm later affected the Philippines and southern China; this image is a historical observation.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 21 December 2010. The tilted day–night boundary gives the Southern Hemisphere longer days. Axial tilt, rather than a change in Earth–Sun distance, controls this seasonal illumination.

credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Sunlit shingle beach and coastal buildings at Southsea, Portsmouth.
caption: Southsea, Portsmouth. Land and sea warm at different rates in sunshine, creating conditions that can support a sea breeze. A photograph of the coast alone does not measure its wind direction.

credit: Dietmar Rabich / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Steam and orange microbial mats around Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park.
caption: Grand Prismatic Spring, Yellowstone. Hot groundwater and heat-tolerant microorganisms create the pool's striking colour bands.

credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
caption: Yosemite Valley, California. Glacial erosion widened and steepened a pre-existing river valley in granite.

credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
caption: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium. The phase is nearly the same for observers in Wales and California at the same instant; local rise times and the disc's orientation differ.

credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
caption: Calciustoll near Ponce, Puerto Rico: a Mollisol with a roughly 30 cm mollic surface over a calcic horizon. Its parent material includes colluvium and weathered limestone.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Sediment circulating in eddies abrades the bedrock, enlarging these potholes.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² colour scale.
caption: This CERES observation maps reflected sunlight. Solar absorption by the Earth system is the incoming shortwave energy minus this reflected component; the image measures reflection rather than absorption directly.

credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer; pumping may lower the water level around a well, which is measured below ground.

credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
caption: Patterned ground in Alaska's Noatak region. The active layer above permafrost thaws and refreezes seasonally; surface patterns show freezing processes, but active-layer depth needs field measurements.

credit: Jesse Allen, NASA Earth Observatory, using data obtained from the Goddard Earth Sciences DAAC. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Parallel rows of clouds extend from sea ice across open water in the Bering Sea.
caption: Cloud streets over the Bering Sea, 20 January 2006. Cold air over warmer water supports convection organised into rolls by the wind.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon. This is a landscape example for tropical rainforest climate; an Af classification is determined from long-term monthly temperature and rainfall, not from vegetation alone.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
caption: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² colour scale.
caption: CERES measures reflected shortwave energy in W m⁻². Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight reflected, so obtaining it requires dividing reflected flux by the corresponding incoming flux; the colour scale here is not albedo.

credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Tilted and folded sedimentary beds exposed at The Settlands coast.
caption: Folded strata at The Settlands, Wales. Trace a bed through the exposure to see deformation recorded in solid rock.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Satellite image of the parallel folded ridges of the Appalachian Mountains and Chesapeake Bay.
caption: NASA Terra MODIS, 15 September 2023. Appalachian ridges and valleys across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania preserve the structure of an ancient mountain belt.

credit: USGS Office of Groundwater / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS map showing the distribution of principal aquifers across the United States.
caption: USGS principal aquifers of the United States, 2000. Colours identify aquifer systems; the map does not show water-table depth or whether a particular well is confined.

credit: Peter Pearson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Grey London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
caption: London Clay forms the lower part of the Naze cliffs. Clay-rich beds commonly transmit groundwater slowly and can act as aquitards; the cliff exposes the material, while permeability is established by testing.

credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: Mantle peridotite enclosed in volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona. It is physical evidence of rock from the upper mantle. The mantle is predominantly solid; local partial melting is not a global magma ocean.

credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 Venus transit. Such alignments require the planet to be near an orbital node. Historical transit timing helped determine the Earth–Sun distance, now represented by the precisely defined astronomical unit.

credit: Gaisarix / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Rounded grey stones and pebbles of different sizes on an English North Sea beach.
caption: Pebbles on the North Sea coast of England. Repeated collisions can round and reduce fragments through attrition; a still image records the resulting grains.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the subsolar point south of the equator and gives southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equatorial plane; the tilt of the boundary is observational evidence, not an angle scale.

credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. The pale E horizon has lost material by eluviation; material may accumulate in the B horizon below.

credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind transports loose sand by surface creep and saltation; the dunes record accumulated transport rather than individual grain paths.

credit: Jan Nyssen, Sander Tielens, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Tigist Araya, Kassa Teka, Johan Van de Wauw, Karen Degeyndt, Katrien Descheemaeker, Kassa Amare, Mitiku Haile, Amanuel Zenebe, Neil Munro, Kristine Walraevens, Kindeya Gebrehiwot, Jean Poesen, Amaury Frankl, Alemtsehay Tsegay, Jozef Deckers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia: published field photographs compare red and black soils along a hillslope. Slope position changes drainage and material movement.

credit: NASA Astronaut photograph from ISS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
caption: The mountains of the Hawaiian islands interrupt the trade winds. Greener windward slopes and drier leeward slopes show the landscape contrast associated with this mountain barrier.

credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat · public domain · resized
alt: Landsat view of the thin Chandeleur barrier islands off Louisiana.
caption: Landsat observations of the Chandeleur barrier islands, Louisiana. Narrow sandy islands separate the Gulf of Mexico from shallow coastal waters; storm erosion can fragment and reshape them.

credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

credit: Kingsmasher678 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
caption: Groundwater emerges at a karst spring in Alabama. Water stored in connected pores and fractures can return to the surface as spring flow.

credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
caption: A mountain basin occupied by glacier ice in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. A basin is a low area bounded by higher ground; drainage basins are defined by the area contributing water to an outlet.

credit: Ustill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · resized
alt: A broad, grassy former river valley near Blumberg, now drained by the much smaller Aitrach.
caption: The Aitrach valley preserves the former route of the Feldberg Danube. Capture by the Wutach diverted its large upstream flow towards the Rhine, leaving the small Aitrach in an oversized valley. The channel itself is difficult to distinguish in this landscape view.

credit: Philip Halling / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Tree roots grow into joints in rock beside a roadside exposure.
caption: Roots grow through existing rock joints. Their growth can widen cracks, contributing to biological and physical weathering.

credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

alt: Deep blue Crater Lake fills a broad volcanic depression, with Wizard Island near its western shore.
caption: USGS aerial photograph of Crater Lake, Oregon. Collapse following the eruption of Mount Mazama formed the caldera; Wizard Island is a younger volcanic cone.

credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag juxtaposes rocks with different geological histories. Such field contacts help reconstruct the Caledonian mountain belt and its crustal terranes; boundaries between terranes need regional evidence as well as one outcrop.

credit: Wilson44691 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Fossilised Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
caption: Ogyopsis klotzi from the Middle Cambrian Mount Stephen Trilobite Beds, Canada. Fossils help correlate and interpret ancient sedimentary rocks.

credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

alt: A pale specimen of kaolinite from Ixtassou, France.
caption: Kaolinite from Ixtassou, France, is a clay mineral. Clay as a soil texture means particles smaller than 0.002 mm; mineral identity and particle size are different properties.

credit: James T M Towill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Weather instruments inside the enclosure at Charterhall in the Scottish Borders.
caption: Charterhall weather station, Scotland. Standardised instruments measure local conditions; climate describes their statistics over many years.

caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

alt: A low shelf cloud sweeps over buildings at Brock University in Ontario.
caption: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
caption: Calciustoll near Ponce, Puerto Rico: a Mollisol with a roughly 30 cm mollic surface over a calcic horizon. Its parent material includes colluvium and weathered limestone.

credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
caption: Floodwater on the Stillaguamish River, Washington. Rain-fed regimes respond to precipitation; a flow's competence is the largest sediment it can move, which cannot be inferred from water colour alone.

credit: NASA Blue Marble / Mdf (projection) · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in the curved-outline Robinson projection.
caption: NASA satellite imagery in Robinson projection. This compromise projection balances several distortions; it preserves neither all areas nor all local angles.

alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
caption: Lava fountains at Kīlauea show magma reaching the surface through a volcanic vent. Its subsurface conduit is inferred from geophysical observations and eruptive behaviour, not visible through the rock.

credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer; pumping may lower the water level around a well, which is measured below ground.

alt: USGS map showing the distribution of principal aquifers across the United States.
caption: USGS principal-aquifer map. Aquifers transmit groundwater; low-permeability aquitards can confine them. Confinement and pressure require a geological section and well measurements, and cannot be read from this surface map alone.

credit: Jean-Marie Vugnon (2) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: The Moselle joins the wider Rhine beside the city of Koblenz, Germany.
caption: The Rhine–Moselle confluence at Koblenz, photographed in 1988. A tributary joins the main channel here.

credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
caption: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows towards the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: Wave breaking at Porto Covo, Portugal. Whether waves build or erode this beach depends on the balance of swash, backwash and sediment transport over time; a single breaking crest cannot establish that balance.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Colour represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

caption: Steppe near Jargalant, Mongolia, far from a moderating ocean. Continental interiors often have larger annual temperature ranges; a weather station's long-term record is needed to measure that range.

alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

caption: NOAA Deep SOLO deployment, 2018. Profiling floats measure ocean temperature and salinity at depth, helping scientists study density structure and deep circulation. The ocean conveyor is a simplified description of a complex circulation.

alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept rain and absorb light for photosynthesis; the photograph shows the living store, not the invisible molecular reactions.

alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: Mantle peridotite carried to the surface as a xenolith within volcanic rock. It provides a sample of solid upper mantle. The lithosphere includes crust and rigid upper mantle; the green xenolith is not a piece of crust.

alt: Metallic black octahedral magnetite crystals on rock, Smithsonian specimen B10614 from Binnental, Switzerland.
caption: Magnetite, photographed in the Smithsonian collection. Pure magnetite loses its spontaneous magnetic ordering near 580 °C, its Curie temperature. This specimen photograph shows the mineral, not a temperature measurement.

alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the subsolar point south of the equator and gives southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equatorial plane; the tilt of the boundary is observational evidence, not an angle scale.

Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equatorial plane; the tilt of the boundary is observational evidence, not an angle scale.

credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep grey beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
caption: The unconformity at Siccar Point records a gap of many millions of years. Ma means million years ago and ka means thousand years ago; those intervals are inferred from geological evidence, not from the photograph alone.

credit: NOAA's National Ocean Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A circular CTD instrument and water-sampling rosette is lowered into the ocean.
caption: NOAA CTD water sampling. Temperature and salinity observations constrain water density and help identify deep-water masses such as North Atlantic Deep Water. The instrument photo does not show the global circulation itself.

credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind transports loose sand by surface creep and saltation; the dunes record accumulated transport rather than individual grain paths.

credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: False-colour Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

credit: NOAA's National Ocean Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A circular CTD instrument and water-sampling rosette is lowered into the ocean.
caption: NOAA CTD water sampling. Temperature and salinity observations constrain water density and help identify deep-water masses such as North Atlantic Deep Water. The instrument photo does not show the global circulation itself.

credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

credit: Jerrod Wheeler (submitted to USGS by Kirk Miller, Wyoming) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
caption: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
caption: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows towards the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
caption: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

credit: Daredeep33 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Turquoise water fills the steep-sided Bimmah sinkhole in Oman.
caption: Bimmah sinkhole, Oman. Dissolution and collapse in soluble rock can create closed depressions called dolines.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
caption: ASTER, 24 September 2005: tributaries dissect sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. A drainage network collects flow towards a main river.

credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer; pumping may lower the water level around a well, which is measured below ground.

credit: Doc Searls from Santa Barbara, USA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial view of elongated low hills around Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin.
caption: Drumlin terrain near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin. The streamlined hills record former glacier flow; they are landforms left after the ice retreated.

credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. The pale E horizon has lost material by eluviation; material may accumulate in the B horizon below.

credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.
caption: NOAA, 11 October–7 November 2015: positive sea-surface temperature anomalies extend across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific during El Niño.

credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

caption: A real USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Read the sheet's coordinate system and scale before giving a position; it is not an OS National Grid map.

caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 Venus transit. Such alignments require the planet to be near an orbital node. Historical transit timing helped determine the Earth–Sun distance, now represented by the precisely defined astronomical unit.

caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system towards the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Net radiation is incoming sunlight minus reflected shortwave and emitted longwave energy at the top of the atmosphere. Positive values indicate a radiative surplus.

caption: NASA Landsat observation of the Thames estuary. The tidal river widens towards the North Sea; pale water reveals suspended material and shallow coastal water.

alt: Wisps of low fog rise above a calm lake on a frosty morning, with trees reflected in the water.
caption: Evaporation fog over a lake. Water vapour mixes into colder air and condenses into droplets; invisible vapour itself cannot be photographed.

alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.

credit: Karthoo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system towards the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: Meanders on Peru's Ucayali River from the ISS. Bend circulation helps redistribute sediment across the channel. A long profile instead plots bed elevation downstream and requires measured heights; this plan view is not that profile.

credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. A landscape photograph shows local relief, ridges and valley slopes.

credit: Leonhard Lenz / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: An exposed soil profile beneath woodland at Wuhlheide in Berlin, with a measuring tape against the face.
caption: Layers in this exposed soil profile differ in colour and texture. These soil horizons record changes in organic matter, weathering and material movement.

credit: GlacierNPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The sharp summit and steep ridges of Little Matterhorn in Glacier National Park, Montana.
caption: Little Matterhorn, Glacier National Park, USA. Glacial erosion on several sides can leave a sharp pyramidal peak; this is not the Matterhorn in the Alps.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
caption: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

credit: Jerrod Wheeler (submitted to USGS by Kirk Miller, Wyoming) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
caption: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
caption: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

credit: NASA/JPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Voyager 2 image of Neptune's blue disc showing cloud bands and the Great Dark Spot.
caption: NASA/JPL Voyager 2 image assembled from green and orange filter observations in August 1989. Neptune is an ice giant; its displayed deep blue is enhanced relative to its natural appearance.

credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
caption: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organise the permafrost landscape.

credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Sunlight passing through Earth's atmospheric limb in an ISS photograph. At low solar angles, light crosses a longer atmospheric path and spreads across a larger surface area.

credit: C.C. Finlay, C. Kloss, N. Gillet / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: Swarm-derived maps compare Earth's magnetic field intensity in 2014 and 2025, with a nanoTesla scale.
caption: Swarm satellite observations constrain Earth's magnetic field. Its main source is the moving, conducting liquid outer core, not a permanent bar magnet; the solid inner core and the core's temperature are inferred from other evidence too.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An SDO observation of the solar photosphere showing a large dark sunspot group.
caption: NASA SDO observes the solar photosphere and sunspots. The Sun supplies incoming solar radiation (insolation). The solar constant is irradiance near 1 AU on a plane perpendicular to the rays, about 1,361 W m⁻²; it is not measured by this visible-light photograph.

credit: USGS · public domain · 14 August 2021 ShakeMap · resized
alt: USGS ShakeMap of the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake with coloured zones of shaking intensity.
caption: USGS ShakeMap for the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake. Intensity varies from place to place and describes shaking effects; magnitude describes the earthquake's overall size. This is the published event-time map, not live hazard information.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept rain and absorb light for photosynthesis; the photograph shows the living store, not the invisible molecular reactions.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
caption: ASTER, 24 September 2005: tributaries dissect sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. A drainage network collects flow towards a main river.

credit: Joshua Stevens / NASA Earth Observatory, Landsat data: USGS · public domain · resized
alt: Big and Little Diomede islands in the Bering Strait, between snow-covered Russia and Alaska, seen by Landsat 8.
caption: Landsat 8, 6 June 2017: Big Diomede (the larger island, left) belongs to Russia and Little Diomede (right) to the US. The International Date Line passes through the water between them; it is a convention, not a visible physical feature.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
caption: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
caption: NOAA photograph of Hurricane Ike damage on the Bolivar Peninsula barrier coast, Texas. Wind stress and low atmospheric pressure contribute to storm surge; the inverse-barometer response is only part of the observed flooding.

credit: Lewis Clarke / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: White chalk cliffs, offshore remnants and a wave-cut base near the Pinnacles in Purbeck.
caption: Chalk cliffs on the Purbeck coast, within the region affected by inversion of the Wessex Basin. The photograph shows the present outcrop; reconstructing earlier subsidence and later compression requires regional geological evidence.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

credit: Richard Sutcliffe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A low grassy coastal terrace below an older cliff near Northbank.
caption: A raised beach at Northbank records former relative sea level. Relative sea level can change through land motion, including glacial rebound, and through eustatic change in global ocean level; the photograph alone cannot separate their contributions.

credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-colour mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
caption: Cassini's natural-colour mosaic of Saturn and its rings. Orbital period depends on orbital size and the central mass. This image shows one system; it does not preserve the scale of distances across the whole Solar System.

credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. A landscape photograph shows local relief, ridges and valley slopes.

credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

credit: NickLongrich / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Exposed layers of the Scollard Formation beside the Red Deer River in Alberta.
caption: The K–Pg boundary in the Scollard Formation, Alberta, Canada. The rock record preserves evidence of the transition around 66 million years ago.

credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025) processed by the European Space Agency and further processed by Josh Willis, and Kevin Marlis/NASA/JPL-Caltech. Story by Emily Cassidy. / Wikimedia Commons · Attribution · resized
alt: Sentinel-6 sea-surface height anomaly map shows lower-than-average levels across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
caption: Sentinel-6 mapped sea-surface height anomalies during La Niña in January 2025. Ocean–atmosphere coupling changes the Walker circulation and can influence distant weather through teleconnections; these atmospheric links are not directly pictured.

credit: Jerrod Wheeler (submitted to USGS by Kirk Miller, Wyoming) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
caption: USGS stream-gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica. A time series from a gauge reveals a hydrograph's rising limb, peak and falling limb. Lag time compares rainfall timing with the discharge peak; it is not a distance along the river.

credit: NOAA GOES-19 / CIMSS, University of Wisconsin–Madison · public domain · 30 October 2025 · resized
alt: GOES-19 satellite view of a cloud-free band beside western Lake Michigan as a land breeze pushes offshore.
caption: GOES-19, 30 October 2025 at 13:20 UTC. A land breeze keeps clouds away from part of Lake Michigan’s western shore. The product combines visible and infrared observations across the night-to-day transition; station measurements confirm the offshore flow.

credit: Paul Wynter / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Graw DFM radiosondes and a radio receiver arranged on a table.
caption: Balloon-borne radiosondes transmit measurements of the atmosphere. Profiles of temperature, humidity and pressure help locate inversions and estimate lapse rates.

credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
caption: NASA Blue Marble monthly composite in an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the equator; parallels run east–west. The geographic reference lines are mathematical, not marks on the land.

credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favour wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
caption: Mississippi levee at Hannibal, Missouri, 20 June 2008. This engineered embankment limits inundation; natural levees instead build up from repeated overbank deposition.

credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
caption: Mississippi levee at Hannibal, Missouri, 20 June 2008. This engineered embankment limits inundation; natural levees instead build up from repeated overbank deposition.

credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton, B.F. Williams, and L.C. Johnson (University of Washington), the PHAT team, and R. Gendler / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A Hubble mosaic of Andromeda's bright central region, dark dust lanes and densely packed stars.
caption: NASA/ESA Hubble mosaic of Andromeda. Resolved stars and dust lanes provide an observed view of a galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away.

credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: Layered rocks at Grand Canyon record the geological carbon cycle and deep time. Lithification converts sediment into rock; the canyon also exposes much older basement in its inner gorge. A landscape photograph alone does not date individual beds.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: Mantle peridotite carried to the surface as a xenolith within volcanic rock. It provides a sample of solid upper mantle. The lithosphere includes crust and rigid upper mantle; the green xenolith is not a piece of crust.

credit: NPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: National Park Service soil scientists examine a freshly sampled soil profile and record its texture.
caption: NPS fieldwork at Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park. Texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay in the mineral soil.

credit: Zdeněk Bardon/ESO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A long-exposure photograph of Orion's stars, red emission nebulae and dark dust clouds.
caption: Orion photographed from ESO's La Silla Observatory by Zdeněk Bardon. Stars that appear close in the sky can lie at very different distances; long exposure reveals faint gas and dust.

credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
caption: Aqua MODIS observed Cyclone Evan near Fiji on 16 December 2012. Its cloud bands spiral around the centre; a mathematical logarithmic spiral is an approximation, not a measured exact fit.

credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: The broad, low-gradient lower Ucayali River seen from the ISS. A river long profile follows bed elevation from source to mouth; this photograph shows the lowland reach, while constructing its profile requires elevation measurements.

credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 metres east of this line.

credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore transport supplies a spit at the Humber estuary.

credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: CERES global map of outgoing longwave radiation with a colour scale in watts per square metre.
caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

credit: NASA Kennedy Space Center, KSC-00PP-0096 · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
alt: The Moon appears copper-red during a lunar eclipse viewed from Merritt Island, Florida.
caption: NASA Kennedy Space Center photograph, 20 January 2000. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; sunlight filtered through Earth's atmosphere gives the eclipsed surface a reddish colour.

credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep grey beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
caption: The unconformity at Siccar Point records a gap of many millions of years. Ma means million years ago and ka means thousand years ago; those intervals are inferred from geological evidence, not from the photograph alone.

credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
caption: Kīlauea, 25 February 1983. USGS photographed a lava fountain approximately 10 metres high; molten rock is at the surface, not throughout the mantle.

credit: NOAA NCEI / CIRES · EMAG2 v3 · public domain · resized
alt: EMAG2 global magnetic-anomaly map with alternating anomalies across the ocean floor.
caption: NOAA EMAG2 v3 maps measured magnetic anomalies. Ocean-floor bands record crust formed under changing magnetic polarity. Matching the pattern to dated reversals supports seafloor spreading and allows a rate to be calculated from distance divided by age; colour alone does not give rock age.

credit: NOAA NCEI / CIRES · EMAG2 v3 · public domain · resized
alt: EMAG2 global magnetic-anomaly map with alternating anomalies across the ocean floor.
caption: NOAA EMAG2 v3 maps measured magnetic anomalies. Ocean-floor bands record crust formed under changing magnetic polarity. Matching the pattern to dated reversals supports seafloor spreading and allows a rate to be calculated from distance divided by age; colour alone does not give rock age.

credit: Thomas Pratt, USGS. Public domain. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS scientists install a field seismometer at Sabana Yeguas, Puerto Rico.
caption: USGS seismometer installation in Puerto Rico. Wave arrival times and recorded ground motion are used to estimate an earthquake's focus, epicentre and magnitude; none of those buried locations is visible in this photograph.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: Mantle peridotite enclosed in volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona. It is physical evidence of rock from the upper mantle. The mantle is predominantly solid; local partial melting is not a global magma ocean.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
caption: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

credit: Mark Reid, USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Wanmei Liang, using data provided by the ARIA team at NASA/JPL-Caltech. The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
caption: NASA ARIA observations of surface displacement following the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. The coloured displacement field is measured evidence of movement, not a photograph of the buried fault.

credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
caption: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows towards the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 metres east of this line.

credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's thin atmosphere above the limb, photographed from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight reveals lower atmospheric layers; coloured bands are not precise altitude boundaries.

credit: Kevin M. Gill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A rounded specimen of augen gneiss with pale mineral eyes enclosed in dark, folded bands.
caption: Augen gneiss: deformation and metamorphism organise minerals into bands around larger crystals. Rock-cycle pathways need not follow one fixed loop.

credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

credit: Richard Webb / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A small stream runs along a valley much larger than its present channel.
caption: A photographed misfit stream. Its present flow is small relative to its valley; former glacial meltwater or a change in drainage may explain the mismatch.

credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
caption: Calciustoll near Ponce, Puerto Rico: a Mollisol with a roughly 30 cm mollic surface over a calcic horizon. Its parent material includes colluvium and weathered limestone.

credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
caption: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: False-colour Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

credit: NOAA's National Ocean Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A circular CTD instrument and water-sampling rosette is lowered into the ocean.
caption: NOAA CTD water sampling. Temperature and salinity observations constrain water density and help identify deep-water masses such as North Atlantic Deep Water. The instrument photo does not show the global circulation itself.

credit: Chris M Morris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A mesquite shrub grows on a mound of trapped sand in the Mojave Desert.
caption: Mesquite in Mojave National Preserve, California. Vegetation traps wind-blown sand and can build a small dune called a nabkha.

credit: Lapos71 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
caption: The first-quarter Moon is near quadrature. Solar and lunar tidal effects then partly oppose, favouring neap tides; the local minimum tidal range can lag the quarter phase and depends on the coastline and basin.

credit: NASA Johnson Space Center / NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A thin sunlit lunar crescent with crater shadows along the terminator against black space.
caption: The Artemis II crew photographed this lunar crescent on 7 April 2026. Phase is the visible fraction of the sunlit hemisphere, not Earth's shadow.

credit: Brian Deegan / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Water falls through a narrow rocky step into a dark plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales.
caption: Cwmorthin waterfall and plunge pool, Wales. Falling water and entrained sediment erode the pool below the step in the river bed.

credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
caption: Seasonal snowmelt feeds a stream near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. A nival river regime is strongly influenced by snow accumulation and melt; this photograph shows a snowmelt source, not a measured annual hydrograph.

credit: Alan Bowring / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Blorenge above Llanfoist, with the shallow Cwm Craf hollow visible on its front slope.
caption: Cwm Craf on Blorenge, Wales, has been interpreted as a former nivation hollow. Persistent snow patches can promote weathering and sediment removal without forming a moving glacier. The foreground hollow lies in a glacial moraine.

credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 Venus transit. Such alignments require the planet to be near an orbital node. Historical transit timing helped determine the Earth–Sun distance, now represented by the precisely defined astronomical unit.

credit: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net). / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
caption: A working sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. A gnomon's shadow connects the Sun's apparent direction with local solar time.

credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
caption: A real USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Read the sheet's coordinate system and scale before giving a position; it is not an OS National Grid map.

credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

credit: Contains Ordnance Survey data © Crown copyright and database right · OS OpenData / Open Government Licence v3.0 · resized
alt: Ordnance Survey 1:250,000 map sheet NO of northeast Scotland with the British National Grid.
caption: Ordnance Survey sheet NO, northeast Scotland. British National Grid eastings and northings are measured from a false origin southwest of Great Britain. Four figures identify a 1 km square; six identify a 100 m square. This reduced 1:250,000 sheet illustrates the system; use a detailed map for precise references.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Sea-breeze air moves inland and helps cumulus clouds develop over the warmer island. Silvery water is sunglint. This daytime image shows sea-breeze effects, not a night-time land breeze.

caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 Venus transit. Such alignments require the planet to be near an orbital node. Historical transit timing helped determine the Earth–Sun distance, now represented by the precisely defined astronomical unit.

alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-colour mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
caption: Cassini's natural-colour mosaic of Saturn and its rings. Orbital period depends on orbital size and the central mass. This image shows one system; it does not preserve the scale of distances across the whole Solar System.

alt: A Hubble mosaic of Andromeda's bright central region, dark dust lanes and densely packed stars.
caption: NASA/ESA Hubble mosaic of Andromeda. Resolved stars and dust lanes provide an observed view of a galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away.

alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.
